20. All things are indeed pure, etc. By saying, that all things are pure, he makes a general declaration; and by adding, that it is evil for man to eat with offense, he makes an exception; as though he had said, — “Meat is indeed good, but to give offense is bad.” Now meat has been given to us, that we may eat it, provided love be observed: he then pollutes the use of pure meat, who by it violates love. Hence he concludes, that it is good to abstain from all things which tend to give offense to our brethren.
He mentions three things in order, to fall, to stumble, to be weakened: the meaning seems to be this, — “Let no cause of falling, no, nor of stumbling, no, nor of weakening, be given to the brethren.” For to be weakened is less than to stumble, and to stumble is less than to fall. He may be said to be weakened whose conscience wavers with doubt, — to stumble when the conscience is disturbed by some greater perplexity, and to fall when the individual is in a manner alienated from his attention to religion.
What is said here proves what is stated in a note on Romans 14:13; that is, that σκάνδαλον is a less evil than πρόσκομμα, only that the idea of stumbling, instead of hindrance or impediment, is given here to the former word. The Apostle still adopts, as it were, the ascending scale. He first mentions the most obvious effect, the actual fall, the extreme evil, and then the next to it, the obstacle in the way; and, in the third place, the weakening of the faith of the individual. The real order of the process is the reverse, — the weakening, then the impediment, and, lastly, the stumblingblock which occasions the fall. — Ed.
Romans 14:22-23
22. Hast thou faith? have it to thyself before God. Happy is he that condemneth not himself in that thing which he alloweth.
22. Tu fidem habes? apud teipsum habe coram Deo. Beatus qui non judicat seipsum in eo quod examinat.
23. And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin.

entries.da0f4b925fac2023d37ee97d4e8d721d5155d2e0: <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.14.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Rom.14.22" sID="gen115788" type="section"/> <div sID="gen115789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22.</hi> <hi type="italic">Hast thou faith?</hi> In order to conclude, he shows in what consists the advantage of Christian liberty: it hence appears, that they boast falsely of liberty who know not how to make a right use of it. He then says, that liberty really understood, as it is that of faith, has properly a regard to God; so that he who is endued with a conviction of this kind, ought to be satisfied with peace of conscience before God; nor is it needful for him to show before men that he possesses it. It hence follows, that if we offend our weak brethren by eating meats, it is through a perverse opinion; for there is no necessity to constrain us.<div eID="gen115789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen115790" type="x-p"/>It is also plainly evident how strangely perverted is this passage by some, who hence conclude, that it is not material how devoted any one may be to the observance of foolish and superstitious ceremonies, provided the conscience remains pure before God. Paul indeed intended nothing less, as the context clearly shows; for ceremonies are appointed for the worship of God, and they are also a part of our confession: they then who tear off faith from confession, take away from the sun its own heat. But Paul handles nothing of this kind in this place, but only speaks of our liberty in the use of meat and drink.<div eID="gen115790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen115791" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Happy is he who condemns not himself, etc. </hi>Here he means to teach us, first, how we may lawfully use the gifts of God; and, secondly, how great an impediment ignorance is; and he thus teaches us, lest we should urge the uninstructed beyond the limits of their infirmity. But he lays down a general truth, which extends to all actions, — “Happy,” he says, “is he who is not conscious of doing wrong, when he rightly examines his own deeds.” For it happens, that many commit the worst of crimes without any scruple of conscience; but this happens, because they rashly abandon themselves, with closed eyes, to any course to which the blind and violent intemperance of the flesh may lead them; for there is much difference between insensibility and a right judgment. He then who examines things is happy, provided he is not bitten by an accusing conscience, after having honestly considered and weighed matters; for this assurance alone can render our works pleasing to God. Thus is removed that vain excuse which many allege on the ground of ignorance; inasmuch as their error is connected with insensibility and sloth: for if what they call good intention is sufficient, their examination, according to which the Spirit of God estimates the deeds of men, is superfluous. <note n="434"> <div sID="gen115792" type="x-p"/> The version of <name>Calvin</name> is, “<foreign xml:lang="la">Beatus qui non judicat seipsum in eo quod examinat</foreign>,” μακάριος ὅ μὴ κρίνων ἑαυτὸν ἐν ᾦ δοκιμάζει; the latter part is rendered by <name>Beza</name>, and <name>Piscator</name>, “<foreign xml:lang="la">in eo quod approbat</foreign> — in that which he approves;” by <name>Doddridge</name>, “in the thing which he alloweth;” by <name>Macknight</name>, “by what he approveth.” The reference is no doubt to the strong, who had “faith,” who believed all meats lawful. The verb means to try, to examine, as well as to approve; but the latter seems to be its meaning here. To approve and to have faith appears in this case to be the same: then to have faith and not to abuse it by giving offense to a brother was to be a happy man, who did not condemn himself. The meaning then most suitable to the passage is this, “Happy the man! who condemns not himself by what he approves,” that is, by eating meat to the annoyance and stumbling of the weak. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen115792" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen115791" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.14.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen115788" osisID="Rom.14.22" type="section"/>

23. But he who is undecided, etc. He very fitly expresses in one word the character of that mind which vacillates and is uncertain as to what ought to be done; for he who is undecided undergoes alternate changes, and in the midst of his various deliberations is held suspended by uncertainty. As then the main thing in a good work is the persuasion of a mind conscious of being right before God, and as it were a calm assurance, nothing is more opposed to the acceptance of our works than vacillation.
The Greek is ὁ διακρινόμενος, “he who discerns,” that is, a difference as to meats; so Doddridge, Macknight, and Chalmers regard its meaning. Beza has “qui dubitat — who doubts,” and so our version. The word used by Calvin is dijudicat, which properly means to judge between things, to discern, but according to his explanation it means to judge in two ways, to be undecided.
The verb no doubt admits of these two meanings; it is used evidently in the sense of making or putting a difference, but only, as some say, in the active voice. There are indeed two places where it seems to have this meaning in its passive or middle form, James 2:4, and Jude 1:22. But as Paul has before used it in this Epistle, Romans 4:20, in the sense of hesitating, staggering, or doubting, we may reasonably suppose that it has this meaning here, and especially as in every place where he expresses the other idea, he has employed the active form. See 1 Corinthians 4:7; 1 Corinthians 11:29,31; etc. — Ed.
And, oh! that this truth were fixed in the minds of men, that nothing ought to be attempted except what the mind feels assured is acceptable to God, men would not then make such an uproar, as they often do now, nor waver, nor blindly hurry onward wherever their own imagination may lead them. For if our way of living is to be confined to this moderation, that no one is to touch a morsel of meat with a doubting conscience, how much greater caution is to be exercised in the greatest things?
And whatever is not from faith, etc. The reason for this condemnation is, that every work, however splendid and excellent in appearance, is counted as sin, except it be founded on a right conscience; for God regards not the outward display, but the inward obedience of the heart, by this alone is an estimate made of our works. Besides, how can that be obedience, when any one undertakes what he is not persuaded is approved by God? Where then such a doubt exists, the individual is justly charged with prevarication; for he proceeds in opposition to the testimony of his, own conscience.
The word faith is to be taken here for a fixed persuasion of the mind, or, so to speak, for a firm assurance, and not that of any kind, but what is derived from the truth of God. Hence doubt or uncertainty vitiates all our actions, however specious they may otherwise be. Now, since a pious mind can never acquiesce with certainty in anything but the word of God, all fictitious modes of worship do in this case vanish away, and whatever works there may be which originate in the brains of men; for while everything which is not from faith is condemned, rejected is whatever is not supported and approved by God’s word. It is at the same time by no means sufficient that what we do is approved by the word of God, except the mind, relying on this persuasion, prepares itself cheerfully to do its work. Hence the first thing in a right conduct, in order that our minds may at no time fluctuate, is this, that we, depending on God’s word, confidently proceed wherever it may call us.
CHAPTER 15
Introduced here, as the conclusion of the last chapter, by Griesbach and other collators of MSS., are the three last verses of the Epistle, 25-27. It appears that the largest number of copies is in favor of this arrangement, countenanced by the Greek fathers, and the Syriac and Arabic versions. In favor of the present order, as in our version, there are some good MSS., the Latin fathers, and the Vulgate, etc. What strongly favors and decidedly confirms the order which we have, is the evident connection as to matter between this and the last chapter, which shows the impropriety of having those verses intervening between them. — Ed.

1. Debemus autem nos qui potentes sumus, infirmitates impotentium portare, et non placere nobis ipsis:

                     <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> Seeing <ns0:hi>all must be judged by Christ, let us no more judge one another,</ns0:hi> but mend this Fault for time to come.</ns0:note>: but judge this rather <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Hi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />therto his Counsel was more general, respecting both the Strong and the Weak. Here he begins in a more parti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cular manner, to apply himself to the more Strong and Knowing Christians; Counselling them to take heed, lest by the Abuse of their Christian Liberty, they should be an Offence to them, that were <ns0:hi>weak,</ns0:hi> and more <ns0:hi>ignorant.</ns0:hi> He entereth upon this with an Elegant Transition, making use of the same Word in a different Sence; for he doth not speak Contraries, when he sayes, <ns0:hi>judge not, but judge</ns0:hi>; for the Word in the former part of the Verse, signifies, to <ns0:hi>condemn</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>censure</ns0:hi>; but here in the following part, to <ns0:hi>deliberate</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>consider. q. d.</ns0:hi> Instead of <ns0:hi>judging</ns0:hi> others, let us look upon this as a Rule for our selves, and our own Deportment, that we <ns0:hi>put no stumbling block,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note>, that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 10.32.</ns0:note> no man put a stumbling, or <ns0:note place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>scandal.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> an occasion to fall in his brothers way <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> Take heed of Offending your <ns0:hi>Brethren</ns0:hi> in any kind; do not, by an unseasonable Use of your Liberty, either drive them from their Christian Profession, or provoke them to imitate you, and so to Sin against their Consciences. You have a Parallel Text, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.9. There he speaks only of a <ns0:hi>stumbling block</ns0:hi>; here he adds an occasion of Falling, or as 'tis in the Original, a <ns0:hi>Scandal.</ns0:hi> Though these two Words do differ in their Etymologies, yet they have one and the same Signification. The Latter word, as <ns0:hi>Stephanus</ns0:hi> observes, is peculiar to Holy Scripture; and seldom, if e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver, used in any common Author, It signifieth properly, the <ns0:hi>Bridge in a Trap,</ns0:hi> which, by its <ns0:hi>falling down,</ns0:hi> catcheth a Creature in a Snare, and so occasions its Ruine; and from thence it is used to denote any thing, which is an occasion to others of <ns0:hi>stumbling</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>falling</ns0:hi>; any thing where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by we so Offend another, as that he is hindered from <ns0:hi>Good</ns0:hi>; drawn into or confirmed in <ns0:hi>Evil.</ns0:hi> Scandal or Of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fence is either <ns0:hi>Passive</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Active; Passive Scandal</ns0:hi> is, when that which is <ns0:hi>Good,</ns0:hi> is by reason of Man's Corruption, an occasion of <ns0:hi>falling</ns0:hi> to him. So Christ himself, and his Doctrine, was a <ns0:hi>Scandal</ns0:hi> to the <ns0:hi>Iews, vid.</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.23., 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.8. <ns0:hi>Active Scandal</ns0:hi> is, when any thing is done or said, which gives occasion of Offence to others, when it is an occasion of Grief, or of Sin to them, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 15.21. This Occasion may be Administred, Either by Evil Counsel, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 16.23. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 2.14. Or by Evil Example, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 9.16. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 15.14. Or by the Abuse of Christian Liberty in things indifferent, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="16">16. Let not then your good be evil spoken of <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Here is another Argument against Offences; it will cause our <ns0:hi>good</ns0:hi> to be blasphemed, or <ns0:hi>evil spoken of.</ns0:hi> Some by <ns0:hi>Good</ns0:hi> here, would understand the <ns0:hi>Christian-Faith,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Gospel</ns0:hi> in general: But Others do rather understand it of our <ns0:hi>Christian Liberty</ns0:hi> in particular. <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> Give none occasion for this great Priviledge of your <ns0:hi>Christian Liberty</ns0:hi> to be traduced; use it so, as that neither the <ns0:hi>weak</ns0:hi> Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stian, nor the Infidel, may Reproach or Accuse you as Licentious or Contentious, <ns0:hi>vid.</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 10.29, 30.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17. For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This Verse contains a New Argument to perswade Christians, not to strive about <ns0:hi>meats,</ns0:hi> or such like things; and that is, That the <ns0:hi>Kingdom of God</ns0:hi> doth not consist in these, but in weightier Matters. By the <ns0:hi>Kingdom of God,</ns0:hi> you may understand the <ns0:hi>Gospel</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>true Religion</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>God<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liness</ns0:hi>; that <ns0:hi>Kingdom</ns0:hi> which God Erects in the hearts of Men, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 17.21. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4.20. When he saith, <ns0:hi>The Kingdom of God is not meat and drink,</ns0:hi> he means, That it doth not stand or consist therein. <ns0:hi>Meat and Drink</ns0:hi> are put by a Synecdoche for all things of an indifferent, or mid<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dle Nature; such things, as the Apostle elsewhese sayes, <ns0:hi>commend us not to God,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.8. They are no part of his Worship and Service; <ns0:hi>The Kingdom of God</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Godliness</ns0:hi> is not promoted, either by the use or the forbearance there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />of, <ns0:hi>vid. Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.6. 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.8.</ns0:note>, but righteousness, and peace, and joy <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Here he tells you Positively wherein the <ns0:hi>Kingdom of God</ns0:hi> consisteth, not in outward Observations, but in inward Graces, and gracious Dispo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sitions. He doth not reckon up all, but Contents him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self with these three, <ns0:hi>Righteousness, Peace,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ioy.</ns0:hi> By <ns0:hi>Righteousness,</ns0:hi> Some understand that which is imputed, of which you read, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 4. Others rather<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> That which is implanted and inherent; it is the same with <ns0:hi>Holiness,</ns0:hi> both the Habit of it in the Heart, and the Exercise of it in the Life. By <ns0:hi>Peace,</ns0:hi> Some think, he means <ns0:hi>Peace</ns0:hi> with <ns0:hi>God,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Peace</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Conscience</ns0:hi>; Others, that he rather means, <ns0:hi>Peace</ns0:hi> with <ns0:hi>Men:</ns0:hi> Or if you will, <ns0:hi>peaceableness,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Christian Concord</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Vnity.</ns0:hi> This suits best with what follows, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 19. and it is often commended to us in Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture. By <ns0:hi>Ioy,</ns0:hi> may be understood, that <ns0:hi>spiritual comfort,</ns0:hi> which ariseth from a present Feeling of the <ns0:hi>Favour of God,</ns0:hi> or from a well-grounded Hope of future <ns0:hi>Salvation.</ns0:hi> As also, the Comfort and Delight which Christians take in the Good and Welfare of each other. He that loveth his Brother, <ns0:hi>r<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>joyceth</ns0:hi> in his Welfare, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.6. and therefore will not <ns0:hi>offend,</ns0:hi> or occasion him to <ns0:hi>Sin.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> in the Holy Ghost <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This is added, to shew the efficient Cause of these Graces, which is the <ns0:hi>Spirit of God</ns0:hi>; and to distinguish this <ns0:hi>Righteousness, Peace,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ioy,</ns0:hi> for that which is meerly Civil and Carnal.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18. For he that in these things serveth Christ, <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> acceptable to God, and approved of men <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This proves the foregoing Assertion, That the <ns0:hi>King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom of God</ns0:hi> consisteth in <ns0:hi>righteousness, peace,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>joy,</ns0:hi> be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> he that <ns0:hi>Serveth Christ in</ns0:hi> and by <ns0:hi>these things, is ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cepted of God, and approved of men</ns0:hi>; this can't be affirmed of <ns0:hi>meat and drink,</ns0:hi> &c. When he sayes, That the <ns0:hi>Serving of Christ in these things, is approved of men,</ns0:hi> he means, Such as are Godly, and of sound Judgment; for of others, they are often hated and reviled for the Exercise of these very Graces: And yet <ns0:hi>righteousness,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>peaceableness,</ns0:hi> have oftentimes their Praise, from the Wicked themselves, <ns0:hi>vid.</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2.26. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 3.4. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 2.52. <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 2.47.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19. Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edifie another <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">This Verse is the Application of the foregoing Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />course, in which you have an Exhortation to the Practise of two great Duties. The one is <ns0:hi>peace,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>peaceableness</ns0:hi>; the other is <ns0:hi>mutual Edification.</ns0:hi> He had perswaded before to <ns0:hi>Peace</ns0:hi> with all Men, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 12.18. And here he speaks more especially of <ns0:hi>Peace</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Concord</ns0:hi> amongst Brethren, <ns0:hi>vid.</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 13.11. <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4.3. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.15. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5.13. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 12.14. This <ns0:hi>Peace</ns0:hi> is very necessary, and Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stians should endeavour all things that will promote it, and avoid all things that will obstruct it. And they must not only live <ns0:hi>peaceably,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>profitably one with another.</ns0:hi> They should Build <ns0:hi>one another</ns0:hi> up in Grace and Know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:430" />20. For meat destroy not the work of God <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Here you have a farther Argument against Scandals<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> For so inconsiderable a matter, as <ns0:hi>eating</ns0:hi> a little <ns0:hi>Meat,</ns0:hi> or for the use of an indifferent thing, <ns0:hi>Do not destroy the work of God.</ns0:hi> By the <ns0:hi>Work of God,</ns0:hi> Some understand the <ns0:hi>Soul</ns0:hi> of a <ns0:hi>Brother,</ns0:hi> that is styled <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>work</ns0:hi> by way of Emi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nency: It was one of the chiefest <ns0:hi>Works</ns0:hi> of the Creation, and made, as it were, with the Consultation of the <ns0:hi>whole Trinity,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Image of God,</ns0:hi> after a sort, was Engraven there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in; and if this be the Sence, 'tis a Repetition of the Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gument in <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 15. Iohn</ns0:hi> 6.29. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 1.3.                <ns0:p n="21">21. <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor <ns0:hi>any thing</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The Apostle proceedeth to enlarge his Doctrine touching this particular, beyond the controversy that oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />c<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>sioned this his discourse; for he sheweth, that to avoid the scandal or offence of our Brethren, we are to abstain, not only from things prohibited by the Law, but also from things that are not prohibited thereby; as from <ns0:hi>Flesh</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Wine,</ns0:hi> or any indifferent thing whatsoever. These words <ns0:hi>(any thing)</ns0:hi> are not in the Original, but they are understood, and well supplyed in our Translation. Thus to do, he sayes is good, as the contrary in the forgoing verse was said to be evil; It is good in regard of God, to whom it is acceptable and pleasing; and in regard of our Brethren, to whom it is profitable and advantageous, the positive (it may be) is put for the comparative; it is good, for it is better: so <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 18.8, 9.</ns0:note> whereby thy bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Some distinguish these three words, <ns0:hi>Stumbled, Offended, made weak</ns0:hi>; making the first to be the greater, and the last the lesser injury: Others will have the first to be the lesser, and the last the greater in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jury. But there are those that think, they all three do signify the same thing; and the <ns0:hi>Syriack</ns0:hi> Interpreter doth render them all by one word, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> is offended: and the same thing may be exprest by divers words, to in<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>inuate the great care we should take, that we do not <ns0:hi>put a Sumbling block</ns0:hi> (as 'tis <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 13.) <ns0:hi>or an occasion of falling into our Bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />th<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>rs way.</ns0:hi> The Apostle seems to practise, what he here prescribeth in 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.13.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22. Hast thou faith? have it to thy self <ns0:note place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>have it <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">

                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> of its self.</ns0:hi> I firmly believe, that now under the Gospel all meats are lawful, and that I have liberty to use or eat what I please; and is it not fit that my practice should be agreeable to my Belief: That I should act ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to my Judgment?                         <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> be professed and acknow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledged, let who will be offended; <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> in indiffe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rent things (which are the subject matter he is treating of) our belief or perswasion therein is not to be unseasona<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bly uttered or declared, so as to occasion scandal or con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tention.</ns0:note>. Happy <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he that condemn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth <ns0:note place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>judgeth <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">

Or else, that doth not inwardly condemn himself, for doing that against his conscience, which he openly alloweth, or practiseth: Such a one is happy in this respect, because he is free from those terrors that torment those who act against their consciences.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23. And he that <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>discerneth and putteth a difference be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tw<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">

                        </ns0:gap>n meats.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> doubteth, is damned if he eat, because <ns0:hi>he eateth</ns0:hi> not of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>because it is not of faith.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> faith <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">In this verse is another Aphorisme respecting especi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ally the weaker Christian. <ns0:hi>He that doubteth of the lawful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of any meat, whether he may or may not eat it, is damn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed if he eat. i. e.</ns0:hi> his own conscience condemns him, or he makes himself liable to damnation, because he eateth not of Faith. By <ns0:hi>Faith</ns0:hi> here is meant knowledge or full per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swasion, as <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> what ever a man doth with a wavering mind, without being perswaded that it is plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing to God, and warranted by his word, he sinneth in the doing of it. He sins that doth any thing against it, though the fact or thing done should not be sinful.
